\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कंकतिका} (kaṅkatikā)}{कंकतिका (kaṅkatikā)}]{\sk{कंकतिका} (kaṅkatikā) — a comb}

\label{lesson:SA-C101-kankatika}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a needle, then the Sanskrit for thread.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कंकतिका}}
\textbf{\sk{कंकतिका}} — \emph{kaṅkatikā} — \textquotedblleft{}a comb\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kaṅkatikā} is \emph{kaṅkata} \textquotedblleft{}comb\textquotedblright{}, already in the Atharvaveda (MW), with the small-thing suffix \emph{-ikā}. CDIAL 2598 calls \emph{kaṅkata} of doubtful Indo-European origin, and it lives on as Hindi \emph{kaṅghī} \textquotedblleft{}comb\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 2598).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kaṅkatikā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{kaṅkatikā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for a needle, then the Sanskrit for thread, then say \emph{kaṅkatikā} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{फेनकम्} (phenakam)}{फेनकम् (phenakam)}]{\sk{फेनकम्} (phenakam) — soap}

\label{lesson:SA-C101-phenakam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for thread, then the Sanskrit for a comb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{फेनकम्}}
\textbf{\sk{फेनकम्}} — \emph{phenakam} — \textquotedblleft{}soap\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{phenaka} is built on \emph{phena} \textquotedblleft{}foam\textquotedblright{} with the suffix \emph{-ka}: \textquotedblleft{}the foaming thing\textquotedblright{}. MW sets \emph{phena} beside English \emph{foam}, an inherited Indo-European word; using \emph{phenaka} for soap is modern, since MW gives it other senses.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{प्रोञ्छनम्} (proñchanam)}{प्रोञ्छनम् (proñchanam)}]{\sk{प्रोञ्छनम्} (proñchanam) — a towel}

\label{lesson:SA-C101-pronchanam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a comb, then the Sanskrit for soap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{प्रोञ्छनम्}}
\textbf{\sk{प्रोञ्छनम्}} — \emph{proñchanam} — \textquotedblleft{}a towel\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{proñchana} \textquotedblleft{}wiping\textquotedblright{} is formed from \emph{proñchati} \textquotedblleft{}wipes off\textquotedblright{}, which MW splits as \emph{pra} + √uñch. CDIAL 9011 finds that link doubtful and suggests the verb is a Sanskritized Prakrit word, perhaps from Dravidian; Hindi \emph{pochnā} \textquotedblleft{}to wipe\textquotedblright{} comes from it. Using \emph{proñchana} for a towel is modern.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{उपनेत्रम्} (upanetram)}{उपनेत्रम् (upanetram)}]{\sk{उपनेत्रम्} (upanetram) — glasses, spectacles}

\label{lesson:SA-C101-upanetram}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for soap, then the Sanskrit for a towel.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{उपनेत्रम्}}
\textbf{\sk{उपनेत्रम्}} — \emph{upanetram} — \textquotedblleft{}glasses, spectacles\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{upanetra} is built from \emph{upa} \textquotedblleft{}near, additional\textquotedblright{} and \emph{netra} \textquotedblleft{}eye\textquotedblright{}; MW explains \emph{netra} as \textquotedblleft{}the guiding organ\textquotedblright{}, from the root √nī \textquotedblleft{}lead\textquotedblright{}. The pairing for spectacles is modern.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{स्यूतः} (syūtaḥ)}{स्यूतः (syūtaḥ)}]{\sk{स्यूतः} (syūtaḥ) — a bag}

\label{lesson:SA-C101-syutah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a towel, then the Sanskrit for glasses.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{स्यूतः}}
\textbf{\sk{स्यूतः}} — \emph{syūtaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a bag\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{syūta} is the past participle of √siv \textquotedblleft{}sew\textquotedblright{}: \textquotedblleft{}something sewn\textquotedblright{}, and MW records it as \textquotedblleft{}a sack, a coarse canvas bag\textquotedblright{}. The root is inherited from Indo-European (EtymDB) and is the same root as English \emph{sew}.
\end{cousinweb}
